I run a small pipeline that publishes technical articles to this blog on a schedule, twice a day, no human in the loop between "check trending topics" and "hit publish." The obvious way to build that is: pick a target count, generate that many articles, post them. I built it that way first. It was a mistake, and not the mistake I expected.

The mistake wasn't quality. The model writes fine prose when it has something to say. The mistake was that "hit the target count" and "have something worth saying" are two different success conditions, and if you only measure the first one, the pipeline will happily satisfy it by rephrasing yesterday's article with a different headline.

The naive version

Here's roughly what the first pass looked like, stripped down:

def run():
    published_today = count_published_today()
    remaining = TARGET - published_today
    for _ in range(remaining):
        topic = pick_highest_scoring_trending_topic()
        article = write_article(topic)
        publish(article)

This runs, it produces output, and every metric you'd naively check — did it run, did it publish, is the count going up — looks green. The failure mode only shows up if you actually read the fifth article of the week and realize it's the third one about the same MCP security checklist with different word choices, because pick_highest_scoring_trending_topic doesn't know it already picked something adjacent to that topic four days ago.

The fix isn't a smarter topic picker. It's giving the loop a legitimate way to produce fewer articles than the target, on purpose, as a first-class outcome instead of an error state.

Making "not enough" a valid answer

The version that's actually running now separates "can I hit quota" from "should I":

def run():
    published_today = count_published_today(api_key)  # UTC day boundary
    if published_today >= DAILY_CAP:
        log("daily cap reached")
        return

    candidates = rank_trending_topics(TAGS)
    prior_titles = load_prior_titles()  # ~30 published, from the work log
    fresh = [c for c in candidates if not overlaps(c, prior_titles)]

    if not fresh:
        # This branch used to not exist. It's the important one.
        log("no distinct angle found, publishing 0 this run")
        return

    n = min(len(fresh), MAX_PER_RUN, DAILY_CAP - published_today)
    if published_today == 0 and is_second_run_of_day():
        n = max(n, 2)  # floor, not a target

    for topic in fresh[:n]:
        publish(write_article(topic))

items.title: Someone Fine-Tuned OpenBMB’s MiniCPM5-1B on Claude Fable 5 Traces to Ship a 657MB Local Thinking Model
items.summary: A community developer, GnLOLot , has published a 1B model that runs fully on local hardware. The model is MiniCPM5-1B-Claude-Opus-Fable5-Thinking , with GGUF builds for llama.cpp-compatible runtimes. It needs no API key and makes no cloud calls. The Proposed Model The model is built on openbmb/MiniCPM5-1B . That base is a real, documented release from OpenBMB . It is a dense 1.08B-parameter model using a standard LlamaForCausalLM architecture. It has 24 layers, grouped-query attention, and a 131,072-token context length. OpenBMB reports 1B-class open-source SOTA within its own comparison set. The base already ships a native thinking template. Reasoning is toggled through enable_thinking , giving both a Think and a No Think mode. The derivative model keeps that template and MiniCPM5’s tool-call format. On top of that base, the developer applied a fine-tune. The card states the model is ‘further fine-tuned on Fable 5 data’ to improve coding and instruction following. The GGUF card repeats this as ‘post-trained on Fable 5 data.’ How it is actually built The described method is not classical distillation. You do not shrink the original model. Instead you generate many conversations with a teacher model. You capture its replies and reasoning traces as text. You then supervised-fine-tune a smaller base model on those traces. This distinction is important for accuracy. Classical distillation transfers signal from a teacher’s logits or weights. No one has access to Claude’s weights or logits. So this is supervised fine-tuning on generated outputs, not weight-level distillation. OpenBMB’s own base model, by contrast, uses a documented On-Policy Distillation stage between its own teacher and student checkpoints. The practical effect is that the 1B model learns to imitate response format and style. It does not absorb the teacher’s underlying capability. A 1B parameter budget cannot hold frontier-scale reasoning. The specs that check out The context window is 128K tokens, inherited from the base config.json (131,072). The GGUF repository ships four quantizations. Q4_K_M is roughly 657MB and is labeled the smallest footprint. Q5_K_M is roughly 751MB. Q8_0 is roughly 1.1GB and is the maintainer’s recommended default. F16 is roughly 2.1GB. The ‘657MB footprint’ is the smallest quant, not the default build. The model loads directly in llama.cpp, Ollama , LM Studio, jan, and KoboldCpp. Interactive: how the build works The explainer below walks the build pipeline, the footprint tradeoffs, and the honest split of what a fine-tune can and cannot carry over. How to run it The GGUF card gives a one-line path through Ollama: Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser ollama run hf.co/GnLOLot/MiniCPM5-1B-Claude-Opus-Fable5-Thinking-GGUF:Q4_K_M The same repository documents llama.cpp, LM Studio, jan, and KoboldCpp. Recommended sampling for Think mode is temperature=0.9, top_p=0.95 . The model may emit reasoning blocks before the final answer, which downstream apps can strip. Key Takeaways The model is a supervised fine-tune of OpenBMB’s MiniCPM5-1B on Claude Fable 5 traces, not a weight-level distillation. Real specs: 128K context, GGUF quants from ~657MB (Q4_K_M) to ~2.1GB (F16), Q8_0 the recommended default. Fine-tuning on outputs transfers format and style, not frontier reasoning or broad knowledge. No benchmarks or training dataset are published, so capability claims are currently unverifiable. Apache-2.0 covers the base weights only; training on Claude outputs raises a licensing question the card leaves open. The post Someone Fine-Tuned OpenBMB’s MiniCPM5-1B on Claude Fable 5 Traces to Ship a 657MB Local Thinking Model appeared first on MarkTechPost .
items.summary_html:
A community developer, GnLOLot, has published a 1B model that runs fully on local hardware. The model is MiniCPM5-1B-Claude-Opus-Fable5-Thinking, with GGUF builds for llama.cpp-compatible runtimes. It needs no API key and makes no cloud calls.

The Proposed Model

The model is built on openbmb/MiniCPM5-1B. That base is a real, documented release from OpenBMB. It is a dense 1.08B-parameter model using a standard LlamaForCausalLM architecture. It has 24 layers, grouped-query attention, and a 131,072-token context length. OpenBMB reports 1B-class open-source SOTA within its own comparison set.

The base already ships a native thinking template. Reasoning is toggled through enable_thinking, giving both a Think and a No Think mode. The derivative model keeps that template and MiniCPM5’s tool-call format.

On top of that base, the developer applied a fine-tune. The card states the model is ‘further fine-tuned on Fable 5 data’ to improve coding and instruction following. The GGUF card repeats this as ‘post-trained on Fable 5 data.’

How it is actually built

The described method is not classical distillation. You do not shrink the original model. Instead you generate many conversations with a teacher model. You capture its replies and reasoning traces as text. You then supervised-fine-tune a smaller base model on those traces.

This distinction is important for accuracy. Classical distillation transfers signal from a teacher’s logits or weights. No one has access to Claude’s weights or logits. So this is supervised fine-tuning on generated outputs, not weight-level distillation. OpenBMB’s own base model, by contrast, uses a documented On-Policy Distillation stage between its own teacher and student checkpoints.

The practical effect is that the 1B model learns to imitate response format and style. It does not absorb the teacher’s underlying capability. A 1B parameter budget cannot hold frontier-scale reasoning.

The specs that check out

The context window is 128K tokens, inherited from the base config.json (131,072). The GGUF repository ships four quantizations. Q4_K_M is roughly 657MB and is labeled the smallest footprint. Q5_K_M is roughly 751MB. Q8_0 is roughly 1.1GB and is the maintainer’s recommended default. F16 is roughly 2.1GB.

The ‘657MB footprint’ is the smallest quant, not the default build. The model loads directly in llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, jan, and KoboldCpp.

Interactive: how the build works

The explainer below walks the build pipeline, the footprint tradeoffs, and the honest split of what a fine-tune can and cannot carry over.

How to run it

The GGUF card gives a one-line path through Ollama:

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
ollama run hf.co/GnLOLot/MiniCPM5-1B-Claude-Opus-Fable5-Thinking-GGUF:Q4_K_M

The same repository documents llama.cpp, LM Studio, jan, and KoboldCpp. Recommended sampling for Think mode is temperature=0.9, top_p=0.95. The model may emit reasoning blocks before the final answer, which downstream apps can strip.

Key Takeaways
  • The model is a supervised fine-tune of OpenBMB’s MiniCPM5-1B on Claude Fable 5 traces, not a weight-level distillation.
  • Real specs: 128K context, GGUF quants from ~657MB (Q4_K_M) to ~2.1GB (F16), Q8_0 the recommended default.
  • Fine-tuning on outputs transfers format and style, not frontier reasoning or broad knowledge.
  • No benchmarks or training dataset are published, so capability claims are currently unverifiable.
  • Apache-2.0 covers the base weights only; training on Claude outputs raises a licensing question the card leaves open.

The post Someone Fine-Tuned OpenBMB’s MiniCPM5-1B on Claude Fable 5 Traces to Ship a 657MB Local Thinking Model appeared first on MarkTechPost.

items.title: Alys Rivers will be a key player in 'House of the Dragon' if her story follows the plot of 'Fire and Blood.' Here's what to know.
items.summary: Gayle Rankin as Alys Rivers in "House of the Dragon" season three. Ollie Upton/HBO Alys Rivers is introduced in "House of the Dragon" season two as a mysterious resident of Harrenhal. In the book, "Fire & Blood," Alys is a mysterious character who's suspected of being a witch. Here's what to know about Alys and her possible future in season three and beyond. Warning: Spoilers ahead for "House of the Dragon" season three, episode five, and for the book "Fire & Blood." Alys Rivers may not be a dragonrider or a soldier, but the self-proclaimed "barn owl cursed to live in human form" is one of the most formidable figures in " House of the Dragon ." Portrayed by Gayle Rankin, Alys is introduced in the HBO show's second season as the unofficial maester of Harrenhal, a derelict castle in the Riverlands held by House Strong. Alys' job is to tend to the noble men within its walls (or whatever's left of them). However, despite her low status, Alys is quickly revealed to be more of a puppet master than a simple servant. Once Daemon Targaryen (Matt Smith) arrives with his dragon to claim Harrenhal, he finds an unlikely ally in Alys. During his time in the castle, Alys gives Daemon potions that seem to induce powerful visions . Using her mysterious influence, she guides the so-called "Rogue Prince" through his doubts, fears, and regrets , culminating in the epiphany that he's not destined to rule. By the end of the season, Daemon has returned to his wife, Rhaenyra Targaryen (Emma D'Arcy), rallied an army in her name, and vowed to help her seize the Iron Throne. Although Daemon and Alys seem to form a bond, she keeps her true agenda obscured until season three. "I've done the queen a service. I put 40,000 Rivermen at her call," she tells Daemon in season three's second episode, titled "Queen's Landing." "Tell her I want Harrenhal," Alys continues. "I've lived there all my long life, and I've seen it given from hand to hand. And yet none seem to cherish it. Why should it not come to me?" Daemon scoffs at her request. Alys is a bastard with no riches, title, or noble husband, which puts her nowhere near in contention for Harrenhal, even if the castle is said to be cursed. He brushes Alys off as a mere midwife. Daemon does promise to speak with Rhaenyra about "some other reward," but his dismissal of Alys may someday prove dire — especially if the series follows her storyline in George R. R. Martin's original book, "Fire & Blood." Here's why Alys is a character to watch in "House of the Dragon" as the Targaryen civil war continues to unfold. Alys is said to be a witch, and no one knows how old she is Gayle Rankin and Matt Smith as Alys Rivers and Daemon Targaryen in "House of the Dragon" season two. Liam Daniel/HBO Daemon's hallucinations at Harrenhal are partly due to the magic of the Old Gods, which is stronger in the presence of Weirwood trees. In the show, Alys seems to manipulate Daemon by channeling this magic. She also seems to have greensight — an ancient ability to see the future through symbolic dreams. (In "Game of Thrones," Jojen Reed is a known greenseer, and some of the Stark children also have green dreams.) She tells Daemon in season two, "You will die in this place," and later, "There are older things in this world than you or I, or living memory. You are not the player, but a piece on the board." She even has intimate knowledge of Daemon's family, including his brother, the late King Viserys . In the book, Alys is not explicitly connected to the Old Gods, but she is widely suspected of having some kind of magic. "Fire & Blood" is written like a history book, wherein the characterizations and narratives often contradict each other. In the case of Alys: "A serving wench who dabbled in potions and spells, says Munkun. A woods witch, claims Septon Eustace. A malign enchantress who bathed in the blood of virgins to preserve her youth, Mushroom would have us believe." Alys' parentage is also unclear. Some assume that Lord Lyonel Strong was her father, which would make her the half-sister of Larys and Harwin — but no one knows when she was born. Alys apparently served as a wet nurse for "countless babes born of other women at Harrenhal," including, possibly, Lyonel himself. Every historian agrees that she was at least 40 when the Dance of the Dragons began, though she looked much younger. It's possible that Alys uses dark magic to keep a young body, much like Melisandre in "Game of Thrones." After Daemon leaves Harrenhal, Alys forms a bond with Aemond Ewan Mitchell as Aemond Targaryen in "House of the Dragon" season three. Ollie Upton/HBO In season three of "House of the Dragon," as in the book, Prince Aemond Targaryen (Ewan Mitchell) flies on his own dragon to destroy Daemon and reclaim Harrenhal — only to find the castle deserted by his uncle. Instead, Aemond finds the castellan of Harrenhal, Simon Strong, and his adult sons. He kills them all. "Thus did the flower of House Strong, an ancient line of noble warriors boasting descent from the First Men, come to an ignoble end in the ward at Harrenhal," the book reads. "No trueborn Strong was spared, nor any bastard save…oddly…Alys Rivers." The "Fire & Blood" historians assume that Aemond sees Alys as "a prize of war." However, they also admit that Aemond seems unusually fond of Alys, particularly given their age gap. (Aemond is about 19 or 20 at this point in the book.) One source claims that Alys used love potions to seduce the prince. Later, Alys becomes pregnant and says she is carrying Aemond's child, "the dragon's bastard." When Daemon finally flies to face his nephew, Aemond brings Alys to the duel on dragonback. Aemond says that Alys told him where to find Daemon — essentially leading both men to their deaths. "She saw you in a storm cloud, in a mountain pool at dusk, in the fire we lit to cook our suppers," Aemond tells Daemon. "She sees much and more, my Alys. You were a fool to come alone." Alys watches from atop Kingspyre Tower in Harrenhal as Daemon and Aemond's dragons attack each other, and, eventually, as they all collapse into the Gods Eye lake and die. She then disappears from the narrative until the Targaryen civil war has ended. After Rhaenyra's fourthborn son, Aegon the Younger, is crowned king (and Aegon II's daughter, Jaehaera, is crowned queen consort as her cousin's bride), rumors begin spreading that Harrenhal is ruled by "a witch queen of fearsome power." Flanked by hundreds of armed men and outlaws, Alys has taken over Harrenhal. She now claims her son is Aemond's trueborn heir, "the rightful king of Westeros." More rumors spread that she has a dragon inside the castle, and that she's able to curse men to death. Before any of the king's men can decide how to end her reign Harrenhal, however, a plague ravages King's Landing and drives Alys from their minds. Her story ends there, and she isn't mentioned again in "Fire & Blood." Ayomikun Adekaiyero contributed to a previous version of this story. Read the original article on Business Insider

Using her mysterious influence, she guides the so-called "Rogue Prince" through his doubts, fears, and regrets, culminating in the epiphany that he's not destined to rule. By the end of the season, Daemon has returned to his wife, Rhaenyra Targaryen (Emma D'Arcy), rallied an army in her name, and vowed to help her seize the Iron Throne.

Although Daemon and Alys seem to form a bond, she keeps her true agenda obscured until season three.

"I've done the queen a service. I put 40,000 Rivermen at her call," she tells Daemon in season three's second episode, titled "Queen's Landing."

"Tell her I want Harrenhal," Alys continues. "I've lived there all my long life, and I've seen it given from hand to hand. And yet none seem to cherish it. Why should it not come to me?"

Daemon scoffs at her request. Alys is a bastard with no riches, title, or noble husband, which puts her nowhere near in contention for Harrenhal, even if the castle is said to be cursed. He brushes Alys off as a mere midwife.

Daemon does promise to speak with Rhaenyra about "some other reward," but his dismissal of Alys may someday prove dire — especially if the series follows her storyline in George R. R. Martin's original book, "Fire & Blood."

Here's why Alys is a character to watch in "House of the Dragon" as the Targaryen civil war continues to unfold.

Alys is said to be a witch, and no one knows how old she isGayle Rankin and Matt Smith as Alys Rivers and Daemon Targaryen in "House of the Dragon" season two.

Liam Daniel/HBO

Daemon's hallucinations at Harrenhal are partly due to the magic of the Old Gods, which is stronger in the presence of Weirwood trees.

In the show, Alys seems to manipulate Daemon by channeling this magic. She also seems to have greensight — an ancient ability to see the future through symbolic dreams. (In "Game of Thrones," Jojen Reed is a known greenseer, and some of the Stark children also have green dreams.) She tells Daemon in season two, "You will die in this place," and later, "There are older things in this world than you or I, or living memory. You are not the player, but a piece on the board." She even has intimate knowledge of Daemon's family, including his brother, the late King Viserys.

In the book, Alys is not explicitly connected to the Old Gods, but she is widely suspected of having some kind of magic.

"Fire & Blood" is written like a history book, wherein the characterizations and narratives often contradict each other. In the case of Alys: "A serving wench who dabbled in potions and spells, says Munkun. A woods witch, claims Septon Eustace. A malign enchantress who bathed in the blood of virgins to preserve her youth, Mushroom would have us believe."

Alys' parentage is also unclear. Some assume that Lord Lyonel Strong was her father, which would make her the half-sister of Larys and Harwin — but no one knows when she was born.

Alys apparently served as a wet nurse for "countless babes born of other women at Harrenhal," including, possibly, Lyonel himself. Every historian agrees that she was at least 40 when the Dance of the Dragons began, though she looked much younger.

It's possible that Alys uses dark magic to keep a young body, much like Melisandre in "Game of Thrones."

After Daemon leaves Harrenhal, Alys forms a bond with AemondEwan Mitchell as Aemond Targaryen in "House of the Dragon" season three.

Ollie Upton/HBO

In season three of "House of the Dragon," as in the book, Prince Aemond Targaryen (Ewan Mitchell) flies on his own dragon to destroy Daemon and reclaim Harrenhal — only to find the castle deserted by his uncle.

Instead, Aemond finds the castellan of Harrenhal, Simon Strong, and his adult sons. He kills them all.

"Thus did the flower of House Strong, an ancient line of noble warriors boasting descent from the First Men, come to an ignoble end in the ward at Harrenhal," the book reads. "No trueborn Strong was spared, nor any bastard save…oddly…Alys Rivers."

The "Fire & Blood" historians assume that Aemond sees Alys as "a prize of war." However, they also admit that Aemond seems unusually fond of Alys, particularly given their age gap. (Aemond is about 19 or 20 at this point in the book.) One source claims that Alys used love potions to seduce the prince.

Later, Alys becomes pregnant and says she is carrying Aemond's child, "the dragon's bastard." When Daemon finally flies to face his nephew, Aemond brings Alys to the duel on dragonback.

Aemond says that Alys told him where to find Daemon — essentially leading both men to their deaths.

"She saw you in a storm cloud, in a mountain pool at dusk, in the fire we lit to cook our suppers," Aemond tells Daemon. "She sees much and more, my Alys. You were a fool to come alone."

Alys watches from atop Kingspyre Tower in Harrenhal as Daemon and Aemond's dragons attack each other, and, eventually, as they all collapse into the Gods Eye lake and die.

She then disappears from the narrative until the Targaryen civil war has ended.

After Rhaenyra's fourthborn son, Aegon the Younger, is crowned king (and Aegon II's daughter, Jaehaera, is crowned queen consort as her cousin's bride), rumors begin spreading that Harrenhal is ruled by "a witch queen of fearsome power."

Flanked by hundreds of armed men and outlaws, Alys has taken over Harrenhal. She now claims her son is Aemond's trueborn heir, "the rightful king of Westeros." More rumors spread that she has a dragon inside the castle, and that she's able to curse men to death.

Before any of the king's men can decide how to end her reign Harrenhal, however, a plague ravages King's Landing and drives Alys from their minds. Her story ends there, and she isn't mentioned again in "Fire & Blood."

Ayomikun Adekaiyero contributed to a previous version of this story.

items.title: Best Local LLMs You Can Run on a Single 24GB GPU in 2026: Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, DeepSeek Compared
items.summary: A single 24GB card is the practical floor for serious local inference. It is enough for genuinely capable models, and small enough to sit on one GPU. An RTX 3090 or RTX 4090 both land in this tier. The card you own matters less than the models you pick for it. The old hobbyist move was to squeeze the biggest 70B quant onto the card. That advice is now outdated. The stronger 2026 strategy uses modern 20B–35B-class models that fit cleanly. These leave room for context, and still respond fast enough for coding, chat, and agents. This guide covers the models that actually fit, why each is worth running, and how 24GB gets spent. How 24GB of VRAM actually gets spent Three things consume memory during inference. Getting the split right decides whether a model fits. The first is model weights . Their size depends on parameter count and quantization. At Q4_K_M, a common home-inference default, each parameter costs roughly 0.58 bytes. A 32B model therefore needs about 18–20GB in weights alone. Mixtral-style Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are the common trap here. Every expert stays resident in VRAM even when only a few route per token. So you size MoE memory by total parameters, never active parameters. The second is the KV cache , which grows with context length. Longer prompts and longer sessions eat more VRAM. The third is runtime overhead from the serving stack . A safe rule of thumb adds roughly 1–2GB for the KV cache and runtime at short context. Quantization is the lever that makes 24GB workable. Q4_K_M is the standard balance of quality and footprint. Q5_K_M and Q6_K raise quality at a memory cost. Q8_0 and BF16 are usually too large for 30B-class models on a single 24GB card. The interactive tool below lets you switch quantization and see each model’s fit change live. &&& The six best local LLMs for a 24GB GPU Every model below carries a permissive license, either Apache 2.0 or MIT. All of them fit a single 24GB card at Q4_K_M with room for context. They are grouped by the job each one does best. Qwen3.6-27B — best all-around and agentic coding Alibaba’s Qwen3.6-27B is the strongest single default for the card. It is a dense 27B model released in April 2026 under Apache 2.0. The release focuses on agentic coding, repository-level reasoning, and frontend workflows. At Q4_K_M it needs roughly 16GB, leaving comfortable headroom for context. Full model cards and the changelog sit in the Qwen3.6 GitHub repository . Qwen3.6-35B-A3B — fastest general-purpose option The Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 35B total parameters and about 3B active per token. It decodes far faster than a dense 35B model because only a fraction of weights fire each step. The memory footprint still tracks total parameters, so plan for roughly 20GB at Q4_K_M. That makes it a tight but valid fit, best when you want speed for general chat and tool use. Gemma 4 26B — multimodal and multilingual Google DeepMind released Gemma 4 on April 2, 2026, under Apache 2.0. It was the first Gemma generation to ship with a fully open license, per the DeepMind Gemma page . The family spans edge models, a 12B unified multimodal model, a 26B MoE with 3.8B active, and a larger dense flagship. The 26B MoE is the natural 24GB pick when you need vision input and 140+ language coverage. Mistral Small 3.2 24B — polished daily assistant Mistral’s Small line targets the everyday assistant workload with low latency. Mistral Small 3.1 added multimodal input and a longer context window, and Small 3.2 refined instruction following. It is a 24B dense model under Apache 2.0, and the lightest footprint in this list at roughly 14GB at Q4_K_M. That headroom lets you push context further than the heavier 32B options allow. In 2026 Mistral also shipped larger successors, but those sit above the single-card tier. gpt-oss-20b — the easy reasoning fallback OpenAI’s gpt-oss-20b is an open-weight reasoning model under Apache 2.0. It is a Mixture-of-Experts design with 21B total parameters and 3.6B active per token. It ships in a native MXFP4 4-bit format, loading in roughly 14GB with generous headroom. It is strong at structured reasoning and tool use, and weaker on broad world knowledge. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B — deepest reasoning, tightest fit DeepSeek distilled its R1 reasoning traces into smaller dense models. The DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B is the 32B variant, built on a Qwen2.5 base and released under an MIT license. At Q4_K_M it uses about 18–20GB, which is the tightest fit in this guide. It exposes its chain of thought through visible reasoning tokens, which is useful for slow, deliberate problems. Ready-made GGUF builds are available from bartowski on Hugging Face . What does not fit on 24GB The frontier open models of 2026 are large sparse MoE systems. They are quite good in performance and reasoning, but they do not run on one consumer card. GLM-5.2 from Z.ai is a roughly 753B-total MoE. Moonshot’s Kimi K2.7 is around 1T total. DeepSeek shipped V4 as a public preview in April 2026, with a V4-Pro checkpoint near 1.6T parameters. Alibaba’s Qwen3.5-397B and Mistral Large 3 sit in the same server-class range. Because MoE memory tracks total parameters, all of these need multi-GPU rigs or high-memory unified systems. They are worth knowing as API options. They do not change what runs on a single 24GB card. How to run these models locally Three runtimes cover almost every setup. Ollama is the simplest path, with automatic quantization selection and an OpenAI-compatible API. llama.cpp gives fine control over GGUF quantization and offload. vLLM is the throughput-focused server for heavier concurrent workloads. Start with one model that matches your main job, not the biggest file you can load. Keep context under control, and let the card do what it does best. Run serious local AI without sending a single token to a cloud endpoint. Key Takeaways 24GB is the practical floor: run right-sized 20B–35B models, not the biggest 70B quant you can squeeze in. Qwen3.6-27B is the strongest single default; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B is the tightest fit at ~18–20GB. MoE memory tracks total parameters, so every expert stays resident even when only a few route per token. Quantization is the fit lever: Q4_K_M is the home default; Q8_0 and BF16 rarely fit a 30B model on one card. GLM-5.2, Kimi K2.7, DeepSeek V4, and Mistral Large 3 are server-class and will not run on a single 24GB GPU. items.summary_html:
A single 24GB card is the practical floor for serious local inference. It is enough for genuinely capable models, and small enough to sit on one GPU. An RTX 3090 or RTX 4090 both land in this tier. The card you own matters less than the models you pick for it.

The old hobbyist move was to squeeze the biggest 70B quant onto the card. That advice is now outdated. The stronger 2026 strategy uses modern 20B–35B-class models that fit cleanly. These leave room for context, and still respond fast enough for coding, chat, and agents. This guide covers the models that actually fit, why each is worth running, and how 24GB gets spent.

How 24GB of VRAM actually gets spent

Three things consume memory during inference. Getting the split right decides whether a model fits.

The first is model weights. Their size depends on parameter count and quantization. At Q4_K_M, a common home-inference default, each parameter costs roughly 0.58 bytes. A 32B model therefore needs about 18–20GB in weights alone. Mixtral-style Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are the common trap here. Every expert stays resident in VRAM even when only a few route per token. So you size MoE memory by total parameters, never active parameters.

The second is the KV cache, which grows with context length. Longer prompts and longer sessions eat more VRAM. The third is runtime overhead from the serving stack. A safe rule of thumb adds roughly 1–2GB for the KV cache and runtime at short context.

Quantization is the lever that makes 24GB workable. Q4_K_M is the standard balance of quality and footprint. Q5_K_M and Q6_K raise quality at a memory cost. Q8_0 and BF16 are usually too large for 30B-class models on a single 24GB card. The interactive tool below lets you switch quantization and see each model’s fit change live.

&&&

The six best local LLMs for a 24GB GPU

Every model below carries a permissive license, either Apache 2.0 or MIT. All of them fit a single 24GB card at Q4_K_M with room for context. They are grouped by the job each one does best.

Qwen3.6-27B — best all-around and agentic coding

Alibaba’s Qwen3.6-27B is the strongest single default for the card. It is a dense 27B model released in April 2026 under Apache 2.0. The release focuses on agentic coding, repository-level reasoning, and frontend workflows. At Q4_K_M it needs roughly 16GB, leaving comfortable headroom for context. Full model cards and the changelog sit in the Qwen3.6 GitHub repository.

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B — fastest general-purpose option

The Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 35B total parameters and about 3B active per token. It decodes far faster than a dense 35B model because only a fraction of weights fire each step. The memory footprint still tracks total parameters, so plan for roughly 20GB at Q4_K_M. That makes it a tight but valid fit, best when you want speed for general chat and tool use.

Gemma 4 26B — multimodal and multilingual

Google DeepMind released Gemma 4 on April 2, 2026, under Apache 2.0. It was the first Gemma generation to ship with a fully open license, per the DeepMind Gemma page. The family spans edge models, a 12B unified multimodal model, a 26B MoE with 3.8B active, and a larger dense flagship. The 26B MoE is the natural 24GB pick when you need vision input and 140+ language coverage.

Mistral Small 3.2 24B — polished daily assistant

Mistral’s Small line targets the everyday assistant workload with low latency. Mistral Small 3.1 added multimodal input and a longer context window, and Small 3.2 refined instruction following. It is a 24B dense model under Apache 2.0, and the lightest footprint in this list at roughly 14GB at Q4_K_M. That headroom lets you push context further than the heavier 32B options allow. In 2026 Mistral also shipped larger successors, but those sit above the single-card tier.

gpt-oss-20b — the easy reasoning fallback

OpenAI’s gpt-oss-20b is an open-weight reasoning model under Apache 2.0. It is a Mixture-of-Experts design with 21B total parameters and 3.6B active per token. It ships in a native MXFP4 4-bit format, loading in roughly 14GB with generous headroom. It is strong at structured reasoning and tool use, and weaker on broad world knowledge.

DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B — deepest reasoning, tightest fit

DeepSeek distilled its R1 reasoning traces into smaller dense models. The DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B is the 32B variant, built on a Qwen2.5 base and released under an MIT license. At Q4_K_M it uses about 18–20GB, which is the tightest fit in this guide. It exposes its chain of thought through visible reasoning tokens, which is useful for slow, deliberate problems. Ready-made GGUF builds are available from bartowski on Hugging Face.

What does not fit on 24GB

The frontier open models of 2026 are large sparse MoE systems. They are quite good in performance and reasoning, but they do not run on one consumer card. GLM-5.2 from Z.ai is a roughly 753B-total MoE. Moonshot’s Kimi K2.7 is around 1T total. DeepSeek shipped V4 as a public preview in April 2026, with a V4-Pro checkpoint near 1.6T parameters. Alibaba’s Qwen3.5-397B and Mistral Large 3 sit in the same server-class range.

Because MoE memory tracks total parameters, all of these need multi-GPU rigs or high-memory unified systems. They are worth knowing as API options. They do not change what runs on a single 24GB card.

How to run these models locally

Three runtimes cover almost every setup. Ollama is the simplest path, with automatic quantization selection and an OpenAI-compatible API. llama.cpp gives fine control over GGUF quantization and offload. vLLM is the throughput-focused server for heavier concurrent workloads.

Start with one model that matches your main job, not the biggest file you can load. Keep context under control, and let the card do what it does best. Run serious local AI without sending a single token to a cloud endpoint.

Key Takeaways
  • 24GB is the practical floor: run right-sized 20B–35B models, not the biggest 70B quant you can squeeze in.
  • Qwen3.6-27B is the strongest single default; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B is the tightest fit at ~18–20GB.
  • MoE memory tracks total parameters, so every expert stays resident even when only a few route per token.
  • Quantization is the fit lever: Q4_K_M is the home default; Q8_0 and BF16 rarely fit a 30B model on one card.
  • GLM-5.2, Kimi K2.7, DeepSeek V4, and Mistral Large 3 are server-class and will not run on a single 24GB GPU.

items.title: I retired early and have been slow traveling for 2 years. I realized I'd been doing it wrong.
items.summary: Kelly Benthall retired early and has been slow traveling; she realized she'd been doing it wrong. Provided by Kelly Benthall After retiring at 53, Kelly Benthall and her husband, Nigel, have been slow traveling the world. An invite to a coming-of-age celebration from their Balinese neighbor changed her view on slow travel. She thought staying longer would create connection. Instead, belonging came from participation. I retired at 53 and have been slow traveling around the world with my husband for almost 2 years. Last month, while we'd been renting a villa in Bali, everything next door would usually grow quiet by sunset. That's when we got a knock on the door. "There will be a party tomorrow night," Kadek told us with his usual easy smile. "It might go a little late." Kadek, our Balinese neighbor, wanted to make sure we knew his family's celebration might continue past 10 p.m. "Don't worry about us," my husband, Nigel, said. In the days leading up to it, we'd watched preparations unfold over the wall: women carrying offerings, relatives arriving, and a miniature boat being built for the ceremony. Kadek couldn't stop smiling whenever he talked about his son's coming-of-age milestone . His excitement was contagious. The following afternoon, he returned carrying a plate of roast pork. "We're celebrating," he said. "Please come." I thanked him, accepted the food, and thought we'd fulfilled our neighborly obligations. Nigel had other ideas. "We should at least stop by," he said. "Just to show our faces." In Bali, the couple got invited to a party at their Balinese neighbor's house. Provided by Kelly Benthall Finding community We'd only lived next door for a few weeks, and walking into someone else's family ceremony felt like showing up uninvited for Thanksgiving. I didn't want anyone to feel obliged to entertain two retired foreigners who happened to be living next door. Still, I followed Nigel through the gate. Only then did I realize we'd been living next door to an ornate Balinese temple. We were staying in the beachside town of Sanur, about 20 minutes southeast of the airport. The smell of roast pork lingered in the courtyard as children darted between chatting relatives. Koko, the neighborhood rescue dog, stationed himself hopefully near the food. Somewhere behind us came enthusiastic singing. It wasn't a band; it was karaoke. In hindsight, the occasional missed note should have given it away. With glasses of fresh homemade tuak, a lightly fermented palm wine we'd been served at the party, in hand, we wandered over. When the men noticed us, they switched from Indonesian songs to familiar sing-alongs like "Sweet Caroline" and "Wonderwall." We insisted they keep singing in Indonesian. They politely ignored us. Benthall singing karaoke with Balinese neighbors. Provided by Kelly Benthall Before long, I was sharing a microphone with one of Kadek's brothers as we sang The Cranberries' "Zombie." Nigel, being British, inevitably chose "Let It Be." Walking back to the villa later that evening, Nigel smiled. "I can't believe you finally did karaoke." "It wasn't karaoke," I said. " It was community. " I'd gone next door expecting to be a guest. Somewhere between Oasis and roast pork, I forgot I was one. A new view of slow travel Until then, I'd assumed slow travel simply meant staying somewhere long enough for connection to happen naturally. I'd been waiting until I felt comfortable instead of finding ways to participate. That night finally helped me make sense of the six months we'd spent traveling through Australia, New Zealand, and Bali. We'd visited breathtaking destinations, but approached all of them the same way. When Nigel and I retired early, we embraced slow travel: renting apartments, staying for weeks instead of days, and living more like residents than tourists. I assumed time would naturally create connection. Instead, we often remained spectators. In Sydney, we spent a day weaving through the crowds around Circular Quay, taking the ferry across the harbor, and sharing a bottle of wine as we listened to music coming from the amphitheater. In Sydney, Benthall and her husband were slow traveling, but not yet finding connection. Provided by Kelly Benthall It was exactly the kind of day I'd planned before we retired. Beautiful, efficient, and memorable. We caught the ferry back to Double Bay with frame-worthy photos — but not a single meaningful interaction beyond ordering coffee and paying for lunch. Christchurch, down in New Zealand, offered the first hint that something different was possible. Our host suggested we volunteer for an afternoon, helping to remove protective sleeves from native saplings so they could continue growing. We barely exchanged more than a few words with the strangers, yet I left feeling more connected to that city than after days of sightseeing. We became regulars at the neighborhood café until our oat milk flat whites were already being made by the time we walked through the door. We walked the trails through Cashmere often enough to recognize the dogs. One morning, a man walking his dog called out, "Hi, neighbor." I looked at Nigel. "Did he mean us?" I was absurdly pleased that he did. Time to take charge Looking back, I realized I'd been asking places to do something only I could do. I thought staying longer would eventually create that feeling. What actually made the difference was joining in. After that evening in Bali , everything became easier. Our housekeeper beamed every morning when I greeted her with another local phrase. The neighborhood children waved us down to chat. Even the rescue dog that used to bark every time I walked past eventually trotted beside me. Benthall in a courtyard hanging out with Balinese kids. Provided by Kelly Benthall The ceremony hadn't changed Bali ; it changed how I moved through it. As Nigel and I plan a five-month trip to South America later this year, our spreadsheet still includes rent, walkability, air conditioning, and laundry. But we're also looking for local cafés where we might become regulars, volunteer opportunities, communities where it's easy to participate, and neighborhoods where life spills out into the open rather than hiding behind resort walls. The morning after my karaoke debut, we sat by the pool drinking tea as conversation drifted over the temple wall. The scooters still buzzed down the alley, the children were still riding their bikes, and nothing about Bali itself was different . Except this time, the language sounded familiar. I still couldn't understand most of the words, but I recognized the voices. For the first time since we'd arrived, they sounded like home. Read the original article on Business Insider

"I can't believe you finally did karaoke."

"It wasn't karaoke," I said. "It was community."

I'd gone next door expecting to be a guest. Somewhere between Oasis and roast pork, I forgot I was one.

A new view of slow travel

Until then, I'd assumed slow travel simply meant staying somewhere long enough for connection to happen naturally. I'd been waiting until I felt comfortable instead of finding ways to participate.

That night finally helped me make sense of the six months we'd spent traveling through Australia, New Zealand, and Bali. We'd visited breathtaking destinations, but approached all of them the same way.

When Nigel and I retired early, we embraced slow travel: renting apartments, staying for weeks instead of days, and living more like residents than tourists. I assumed time would naturally create connection.

Instead, we often remained spectators.

In Sydney, we spent a day weaving through the crowds around Circular Quay, taking the ferry across the harbor, and sharing a bottle of wine as we listened to music coming from the amphitheater.

In Sydney, Benthall and her husband were slow traveling, but not yet finding connection.

Provided by Kelly Benthall

It was exactly the kind of day I'd planned before we retired. Beautiful, efficient, and memorable. We caught the ferry back to Double Bay with frame-worthy photos — but not a single meaningful interaction beyond ordering coffee and paying for lunch.

Christchurch, down in New Zealand, offered the first hint that something different was possible. Our host suggested we volunteer for an afternoon, helping to remove protective sleeves from native saplings so they could continue growing.

We barely exchanged more than a few words with the strangers, yet I left feeling more connected to that city than after days of sightseeing.

We became regulars at the neighborhood café until our oat milk flat whites were already being made by the time we walked through the door. We walked the trails through Cashmere often enough to recognize the dogs.

One morning, a man walking his dog called out, "Hi, neighbor."

I looked at Nigel.

"Did he mean us?"

I was absurdly pleased that he did.

Time to take charge

Looking back, I realized I'd been asking places to do something only I could do. I thought staying longer would eventually create that feeling. What actually made the difference was joining in.

After that evening in Bali, everything became easier. Our housekeeper beamed every morning when I greeted her with another local phrase. The neighborhood children waved us down to chat. Even the rescue dog that used to bark every time I walked past eventually trotted beside me.

Benthall in a courtyard hanging out with Balinese kids.

Provided by Kelly Benthall

The ceremony hadn't changed Bali; it changed how I moved through it.

As Nigel and I plan a five-month trip to South America later this year, our spreadsheet still includes rent, walkability, air conditioning, and laundry. But we're also looking for local cafés where we might become regulars, volunteer opportunities, communities where it's easy to participate, and neighborhoods where life spills out into the open rather than hiding behind resort walls.

The morning after my karaoke debut, we sat by the pool drinking tea as conversation drifted over the temple wall. The scooters still buzzed down the alley, the children were still riding their bikes, and nothing about Bali itself was different.

Except this time, the language sounded familiar. I still couldn't understand most of the words, but I recognized the voices. For the first time since we'd arrived, they sounded like home.
